p.fact: **Scope of this document.** This file is the maintainer's operating guide: the *shape of a normal day* (commit on mainline, fan out at natural checkpoints), *handling reported drift* (investigate, reconcile into mainline, re-fan — never clobber), *onboarding a host*, and *offboarding a host*.
The model behind it is in [`SOURCE-MIRRORS-PROTOCOL.md`](SOURCE-MIRRORS-PROTOCOL.md); the machinery in [`fanout-mechanics.md`](fanout-mechanics.md).

quote.fact: A change arrives somewhere → you review and accept it there → you bring it into local `main` → you fan out → it is everywhere.

p.fact: Everything below is that sentence, expanded.

section.title: A normal day

p.fact: You work on mainline the way you always have.
Commit locally, in atomic commits, with well-formed messages.
Nothing about being multi-homed changes how you *author* history.
What is new is one habit: **fan out at natural checkpoints.**
Not after every commit — after a coherent unit of work, the same moments you would have pushed in a single-host project:

td.fact: Fan out as the wind-down step
Before stepping away for a while

section.fence: # ... a session's worth of commits on mainline ... project-mirror --check # optional: confirm where the hosts stand project-mirror # push main + tags to every host, ff-only

p.fact: The fan-out is a **deliberate act, not a daemon.**
There is no background job racing your commits to the hosts; you decide when the world sees the new history.
That is what keeps mainline the single writer — nothing pushes but you, when you say so.

section.title: Integrating an accepted change

p.fact: A contribution reaches mainline one of two ways, depending on where you accepted it:

item.fact: **You merged it via a host's web UI.** That host's `main` is now ahead. Bring it home *before* fanning out:

section.fence: git fetch <that-host-url> main git merge --ff-only FETCH_HEAD project-mirror

p.fact: See [`fanout-mechanics.md` §bring-home](fanout-mechanics.md#bring-home).

item.fact: **You integrate locally** — a fork branch, or an emailed patch. On `main` with a clean tree:

section.fence: git fetch <contributor-url> <their-branch> # or: git am < patch.eml git merge --ff-only FETCH_HEAD # or your chosen merge project-mirror

p.fact: Either way, the shape is identical: the change lands in **mainline first**, and only the fan-out puts it on the hosts.
A web-UI "Merge" button is an *inbox event*, not integration.

section.title: Handling reported drift

p.fact: `--check` (or a host warning) reports **DRIFT** on a host: it carries a `main` your mainline does not.
Almost always this is a direct write or a force-push to that host — exactly the thing the model forbids, surfaced loud instead of silently reconciled.
Do **not** re-run the fan-out hoping it clears.
It will not — the fan-out refuses to force, by design.
Reconcile deliberately:

item.fact: **Investigate.** Fetch the host and look at what it has that you do not.

section.fence: git fetch <host-url> main git log --oneline main..FETCH_HEAD # the host's extra commits

item.fact: **Decide.** Are those commits wanted? Usually someone pushed a real fix directly. Sometimes it is junk to discard.
**Reconcile *into* mainline.** Merge or cherry-pick the wanted commits onto mainline. Now mainline is ahead of the host again.

section.fence: git merge FETCH_HEAD # or cherry-pick the good ones

item.fact: **Re-fan.** `project-mirror` — the host fast-forwards cleanly, because mainline now contains its history.

quote.fact: A diverged target is a signal to investigate, never something to silently clobber.

p.fact: The one thing you never do is "fix" drift by overwriting the host to match mainline.
That discards whatever real work caused the drift — which is precisely the data the loud failure was protecting.
Adding a host is deliberately small:

item.fact: **Create an empty repo** on the new host (no README, no initial commit — it must be empty so the first fan-out is a clean fast-forward from nothing).
**Add one manifest entry** — name, url, mode, refs — and commit it. The commit is the audit trail for "when did this host join".
**Ensure access** — your key can push to it (`push` mode), or the host is configured to mirror itself (`self-pull` mode).
**First fan-out.** `project-mirror`. The new host receives the full history; every existing host is a no-op.

p.fact: That is the entire onboarding.
No re-architecture, no cutover — the model was built for the host set to be *living*.
Removing a host is smaller still:

item.fact: **Delete its `[[target]]` entry** from the manifest and commit the removal. The fan-out stops targeting it immediately.
**Optionally archive the host copy** — leave it read-only as a historical mirror, or delete the repo on that host.

p.fact: Nothing is lost either way: **every remaining host holds the full history of the declared refs, and mainline holds the whole tree.**
Offboarding a mirror never subtracts a commit from the project — it only stops one replica from being kept current.
That is the payoff of "every host is a complete replica": the host set can shrink as freely as it grew.

item.fact: Author on mainline as normal; fan out at natural checkpoints, never as a background daemon.
A change lands in mainline *first*; the fan-out is what puts it on the hosts. A web-UI merge is an inbox event, not integration.
Drift is investigated and reconciled *into* mainline, then re-fanned — never cleared by clobbering the host.
Onboard a host: empty repo → one manifest entry → first fan-out. Offboard: remove the entry, optionally archive the copy.

Every host holds the full history of the refs the manifest declares for it (`main` + tags today; any deliberately declared branch later), so the set grows and shrinks without data loss. Refs outside that set live only where they were authored — the fan-out is replication of a declared line, not a backup of the whole tree.
